source.version: Journal version of record: Nature Human Behaviour, Volume 8, October 2024, pp. 1906-1914; doi 10.1038/s41562-024-01953-1; received 11 September 2023, accepted 10 July 2024, published online 12 August 2024. PDF pp. 10-12 hold the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary (last updated by authors Jun 13, 2024). The markdown conversion holds the main text, references, back matter and Reporting Summary (md lines 271-523), but it renders Table 1 and Fig. 1 as loose picture text, places the second half of the Experiment 3 Methods before the Experiment 2B Methods, and drops the Reporting Summary check boxes (the ticked n/a box for per-group sample sizes shows only on PDF p. 10).
source.title_on_document: An empirical investigation of the impact of ChatGPT on creativity

supplement.where: Online supplementary material at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-024-01953-1 (PDF p. 9, Additional information); data and code at https://osf.io/rzn87/ (PDF p. 8, Data availability and Code availability).
supplement.holds: Supplementary Notes A-K, as the main text cites them: lay and pilot surveys (A, B), survey materials (C), sample responses (D), originality and appropriateness sub-dimension analyses for all experiments (E; the main text prints only Experiment 1's sub-dimension tests, without arm means), share of top-ranked ideas in Experiment 1 (F; the main text gives only its direction), details of every expert-judge analysis, including articulateness, verbosity, the Experiment 2B newness type (the main text gives no numbers and names no arms) and the Experiment 3 expert mediation (G; the main text omits expert arm means in Experiment 2A and expert s.d.s in Experiment 2B), modification analyses (H), Experiment 3 process and exploratory measures and PANAS (I), the list of nine constraints (J), the empathy manipulation check (K). Per-arm participant counts are in neither the main text nor the Reporting Summary.

paper_design_summary: Six online experiments (labelled 1, 2A, 2B, 3, 4 and 5; the abstract counts five) with US MTurk or Prolific participants. Individuals were randomly assigned to use ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) or a comparison aid while writing an idea for an everyday product problem: Google Web search (Experiments 1, 2A, 3, 4, 5) or no aid (Human-only; Experiments 2A and 2B); Experiments 4 and 5 cross the technology factor with constraint level or empathy framing, and Experiment 2B adds 100 unedited ChatGPT responses with no participant. Separate panels of lay judges rated each idea on originality and appropriateness (averaged into a creativity score), and three expert judges rated the ideas as a robustness check.

outcomes.name: Creativity score rated by lay judges
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: 331 MTurk judges; three originality items (original/innovative/creative) and three appropriateness items (practical/effective/useful), 1-7, averaged (alpha = 0.96). Idea scores averaged to one score per participant. The share of ideas with top-ranked scores, whose direction the main text reports, is coded as S1-O6.

contrasts.reported: M ChatGPT-assisted = 4.28, s.d. = 0.81 versus M Web-search-assisted = 3.89, s.d. = 0.80; two-sided t-test: t231 = 3.68; P = 2.87 x 10^-4; Cohen's d = 0.49; 95% CI (0.22, 0.75). Arm ns not printed.

outcomes.name: Creativity score rated by lay judges, participant arms (ChatGPT-assisted vs Human-only)

outcomes.measure_detail: 241 Prolific judges; same six-item scale as Experiment 1 (alpha = 0.95). One idea per participant, so the printed arm means and s.d.s describe participants. contrasts.reported: M ChatGPT-assisted = 4.84, s.d. = 0.47 versus M Human-only = 3.66, s.d. = 0.89; t297 = 13.30; P = 5.56 x 10^-32; d = 1.88; 95% CI (1.56, 2.20). One-way ANOVA over the three conditions F2,297 = 117.00, P = 4.36 x 10^-38, partial eta2 = 0.44. Arm ns not printed.

eligibility.reason: All six experiments randomly assign individual US online participants (Qualtrics randomizers) to ChatGPT versus Google Web search and/or a no-aid Human-only arm (Methods, PDF pp. 6-8; Reporting Summary, PDF p. 11). Each analyzes 194 to 400 people, well above 50. The outcome is a creativity score that lay judges (and, as a robustness check, three expert judges) gave each submitted idea, written while ChatGPT was available. Per-arm counts are not printed. Experiment 2B also compares 100 unedited ChatGPT responses (no participants) with human ideas; that comparison is ai_vs_human context. Experiment 2B tests its randomized arms in a model that also holds those 100 responses (t297), which makes those outcomes' unit output but leaves all three criteria met.

one_line_finding: Across six online experiments, lay judges rated ideas produced with ChatGPT more creative than ideas produced with Google search (Cohen's d = 0.32 to 1.01) or with no aid (d = 0.56 in Experiment 2A, 1.88 in Experiment 2B) (Table 1, PDF p. 5, journal p. 1910).
open_questions: Per-arm and per-cell participant counts are printed for no experiment, and the Reporting Summary marks the per-group sample-size item 'n/a' (PDF p. 10); the OSF data (https://osf.io/rzn87/) may hold them.

Experiment 2B: the tests of the randomized arms (t297) and the one-way ANOVA (F2,297) run over 300 ideas, including the 100 ChatGPT-only responses that no participant wrote, so their error term pools variance from AI-only outputs, and the text does not say how the printed d values (1.88 lay, 1.77 expert) were computed. A two-arm participant-level effect needs the arm ns, which the OSF data may hold.
Experiment 2B: the ChatGPT-only s.d. is 0.40 in Table 1 and in the first Results mention but 0.30 in the ChatGPT-assisted versus ChatGPT-only sentence (PDF p. 3).

Experiment 2B newness type: expert judges classified ideas as not new, incrementally new or radically new, but the main text gives no numbers, does not say whether 'ChatGPT' means the ChatGPT-assisted ideas, the ChatGPT-only responses or both, and names no comparison group. The result is therefore not coded as an outcome (it was S3-O3 in the reconciled form); Supplementary Note G holds the details.

Experiments 4 and 5: each printed 2 x 2 ANOVA 'main effect' of technology matches one simple effect (Experiment 4: sqrt(5.06) = 2.25 and P = 0.025, as for the High-constraint t396; Experiment 5: sqrt(49.26) = 7.02 and P = 1.04 x 10^-11, as for the Baseline-empathy t379), so the form records it with that simple effect and codes no separate contrast. No lay-judge contrast pooled over both levels of the second factor is printed; the OSF data and code would give one and show how the 'main effect' was computed.
Experiment 4: Table 1 labels the fourth row (4.40, s.d. 0.61) 'ChatGPT-assisted x Low constraints'; the Results text (PDF p. 4) gives it as the Web-search-assisted low-constraint cell.

The Reporting Summary (PDF p. 11) attributes the G*Power power analysis to Experiment 2A and also lists 2A among the experiments with no sample-size method, while Methods (PDF p. 7) attributes it to Experiment 2B; its Data exclusions line gives no count for 2B although 216 finished and 200 were analyzed. The 2B preregistration (https://aspredicted.org/J7P_ZFN) and the OSF data may settle both points.
Experiment 3 judges are described with the same mean age and percent female as the participants (43.11 years; 50 percent female), PDF pp. 3 and 7; possibly a copy error.

Experiment 1 Methods print t231 = 1.42 with P = 0.149 for the number of ideas (PDF p. 6); a two-sided t of 1.42 on 231 degrees of freedom gives P of about 0.157, so one of the two numbers may be misprinted. Not resolved from the document.
Preregistration is not stated for Experiments 1 and 3; the Reporting Summary lists 2A, 2B, 4 and 5 only.

Supplementary Notes E to I are not in this PDF. The main text points to them for the sub-dimension results of all experiments (E), the Experiment 1 share of top-ranked ideas, whose direction alone is printed (F; coded as S1-O6), the details of every expert-judge analysis, including the Experiment 2B newness type (G), the modification analyses (H) and the Experiment 3 process measures (I).
notes: The paper reports no similarity or diversity measure across participants and no outcome produced after AI was removed, so its outcomes answer only with_ai; Experiment 2B adds two ai_vs_human outcomes coded question none (S3-O4, S3-O5). The abstract says 'five experiments'; the paper reports six (1, 2A, 2B, 3, 4, 5). Units: Experiment 1 averages each participant's idea scores, and the t-test degrees of freedom in Experiments 1, 2A, 3, 4 and 5 equal people analyzed minus the number of cells, so those outcomes are coded participant; S1-O6, a share of ideas, is coded output. Experiment 2B also collects one idea per participant, but every Experiment 2B test is a contrast in a three-group model over 300 ideas (t297, F2,297), 100 of which are ChatGPT-only responses with no participant, so all four Experiment 2B outcomes are coded output with n_units 300. Arm means and s.d.s are printed but arm ns are not, so arm_means_sds_ns is never checked. Lay judges came from the same panel as participants (MTurk n = 331 and 158; Prolific n = 232, 241, 321 and 310); expert judges were three professionals in every experiment. The paper has more than 15 outcomes scored on the output. This form lists every outcome with a main-text result whose arms the text names: 16 with_ai outcomes plus the 2 ai_vs_human outcomes, 18 in all, more than the 15 the form-spec asks for. It leaves out results reported only in the Supplementary Notes: sub-dimension results for Experiments 2A-5 (Note E), expert articulateness and verbosity ratings, and the Experiment 3 expert creativity ratings, whose ChatGPT versus Web search contrast the main text does not print (Note G; the main text prints only the expert mediation indirect effect, 0.20, 95% CI (0.09, 0.34)). It also leaves out the Experiment 2B newness-type result: expert judges classified each idea as not new at all, incrementally new or radically new, and the main text says only that 'ChatGPT is particularly effective at generating incrementally new ideas but less effective at generating radically new ideas', with no numbers, no named arms and no comparison group (PDF p. 3; Note G). Also not coded as outcomes: Experiment 3 self-reported idea exposition aid (M 5.16, s.d. 1.96 versus 2.94, s.d. 1.59; t192 = 8.69; d = 1.25; PDF pp. 3-4) and the other self-reports and PANAS (Note I), the serial-mediation indirect effects, the Experiment 2B correlation between self-reported modification and creativity (r = 0.11, P = 0.291), and the lay and pilot surveys (Notes A and B), which measure attitudes. Other document inconsistencies: Experiment 2B Methods say participants were randomly assigned to 'one of two conditions' while Results call the design three-level (the third level is AI-only output); Experiment 4 Results say participants 'were assigned' while Methods say 'randomly assigned'; Experiment 1 Results describe the experts as having at least 5 years of experience in businesses, product management and consulting, Methods as more than 5 years in product management, consulting and business strategy. Both raw forms omitted source.supplement; the reconciler added it. Final pass, after the challenge checks: S3-O1 and S3-O2 recoded from participant to output with n_units 300; S3-O3 (newness type) removed, with the other outcome ids kept, so S3 has no S3-O3; the separate 2 x 2 'main effect' contrasts removed from S5-O1 and S6-O1, because each equals one simple effect (their statistics are in measure_detail); S1-O6 added; how_used for S3, S5 and S6 now reports instructions, not observed use; source.version corrected. Also in the final pass: the S3 'who' and ai_tool fields say the 98.04 percent GPT-3.5 share has no denominator (98.04 percent of 200 is not a whole number); the S3 exclusions say 200 analyzed; sample_overlap now quotes c015 itself. PDF pp. 1-9 = journal pp. 1906-1914; PDF pp. 10-12 = Reporting Summary. In 'reported' strings, exponents are written as 10^-4.
